text:
elie: Bringing up whirl9b (int4) on Dedicated pools — intermittent OOMs when clients hit long generations. Seen during canary and a small fleet run. Logs show large KV allocations around token 800-1200 for some requests. Anyone seen this pattern before?

sam: Can you paste the logs snippet and the serving config you used? quick guess: batch sizing or max_new_tokens too high.

elie: Paste logs below — truncated: 
```
[2026-03-22T14:03:12Z] request_id=abc123 model=whirl9b-int4 seq_len=96 max_new_tokens=1024 batch_size=4 mem_used=12.4GB kv_alloc_delta=3.8GB
[2026-03-22T14:03:12Z] gpu0: oom during kv_alloc at /serving/runtime/kv_cache.cpp:412
[2026-03-22T14:03:12Z] fallback: evicting prefix, reclaimed=256MB, retry -> success
```
Config that triggered it: 
```yaml
model: whirl9b-int4
batching:
  max_batch_size: 4
  max_concurrent: 8
runtime:
  max_new_tokens_default: 1024
  kv_eviction_policy: lazy
```

perf-bot: Snapshot for canary (whirl9b-int4 @ pool-canary): p50=140ms, p95=340ms, p99=1.8s, OOMs=3 in last 30m, avg_tokens_per_req=420 

jia: fwiw, during the int4 quant eval I ran yesterday on the same checkpoints we saw a small but consistent quality regression on long-form summarization tasks — rougeL down ~2.2 pts vs fp16. Might be related because quantized outputs diverge on long generations.

oliver: Two angles: 1) operational — KV / batch pressure; 2) quality — quant / max_new_tokens interplay. Are customers frequently hitting >512 tokens? If so we should set safer defaults.

elie: Agreed. Quick test: reduced batch & hard cap in canary, enabled slot compactor, and switched eviction to eager. Patch I applied: 
```yaml
batching:
  max_batch_size: 2
  max_concurrent: 6
runtime:
  max_new_tokens_default: 256
  kv_eviction_policy: eager
  kv_compactor: enabled
  kv_eviction_threshold: 0.55
```
Rolled at 14:15.

perf-bot: Canary update @ 14:45: p99 down to 1.1s, OOMs=0 in last 30m, avg_mem_headroom increased by ~1.8GB.

sam: Nice. Did reducing max_new_tokens change end-user quality metrics?

jia: I ran a quick eval subset (200 prompts mix long/short). With max_new_tokens=256, int4 rougeL gap vs fp16 reduced to ~1.0 pt on long prompts (previously ~2.2). Hypothesis: int4 drift compounds over very long contexts; limiting generation length and batching reduces stress and gives more consistent outputs.

oliver: Actionable plan suggestion:
- Default for whirl9b-int4: max_new_tokens_default=256, max_batch_size=2
- Enable kv_compactor and eager eviction by default for this model family
- Add a per-route override for customers who explicitly need longer generations (with a warning + concurrency cap)
- Run a formal quant sweep: int8 vs int4 hybrid for long-form tasks

elie: Done a quick follow-up: created ticket WL-5421 for the defaults + rollout notes, and WL-5422 for quant sweep. Also added a canary monitor for avg_tokens_per_req > 400 to auto-throttle or route to a larger (fp16) variant.

sam: One more operational note — we saw fragmentation spikes when sequences are highly variable within the same batch. If we can gate batching by request max_new_tokens (i.e., prefer grouping similar-length requests) it helps. There's a batching heuristic prototype in repo:
```py
# pseudo
def choose_batch(requests):
  group = bucket_by_max_new_tokens(requests, bins=[0,128,256,512,1024])
  return pick_best_group(group)
```

jia: I'll run the full eval sweep tomorrow (int4/int8/hybrid) and post a matrix with rouge/bleu and latency/cost. Expected timeline: 48h.

oliver: Sounds good. If sweep shows quality gap still >1.5 pts for int4 on long-form, we should surface fp16 fallback policy in console for customers.

elie: Canary stable for now, no OOMs for 2.5h after the patch. :thumbsup: I'll add a short SOP for on-call: lower batch cap, reduce default max_new_tokens, enable compactor, escalate if OOMs persist.

(End)
